title: Small Red Cells: Iron Deficiency, Thalassemia Trait and Inflammation
summary: Watch a smear turn small, pale and unequal as iron runs out, then crowd with small even cells in thalassemia trait — and sort them with ferritin, the Mentzer index and HbA2.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 33 Hit 1 (core: iron deficiency by ferritin), Hits 7, 10 and 18, Trap 1 and the iron-deficiency / inflammation / thalassemia-trait comparison table. Uses WHO 2020 ferritin cut-offs (< 15 µg/L; < 70 µg/L in inflamed adults) alongside the reviewer’s < 12 and < 50–60 figures (register flag rv-ferritin-cutoffs).

objectives: Use ferritin to diagnose iron deficiency, including the higher cut-off when inflammation is present.
Distinguish iron deficiency, anemia of inflammation and thalassemia trait from the iron panel, RBC count and MCV.
Calculate and interpret the Mentzer index, and confirm β-thalassemia trait with HbA2.

scenes.title: Two small-cell anemias, one wrong pill
scenes.altText: Two patients with the same low MCV (small red cells). A bottle of iron pills hovers over both. One smear shows few, pale, unequal cells; the other shows many small, even cells. The cartoon scientist asks: should both get iron?

cues.text: Two patients both have small red cells — a low MCV.
The easy move is to give both of them iron. For one patient, that is exactly right. For the other, it does nothing — and extra iron can even build up.
The lab can tell them apart before anyone swallows a pill. Here’s how.

keys.label: Iron for both? ✗ not so fast

scenes.title: Ferritin: the iron savings account
scenes.altText: A bank-vault cartoon labelled “ferritin = stored iron”. Normal stores show a full vault. In iron deficiency the vault empties first; a WHO cut-off line reads “< 15 µg/L = iron deficiency (apparently healthy adults)”. A second line, for adults with infection or inflammation, sits higher at “< 70 µg/L”. Then the smear shifts from normal (even, normal-sized cells) to iron-deficient: fewer cells, smaller, paler, more unequal.

cues.text: The body banks iron in a protein called ferritin. A little ferritin leaks into the blood, and the amount tracks the size of the savings.
When iron runs short, the savings empty first. WHO uses a ferritin below 15 micrograms per litre to diagnose iron deficiency in otherwise healthy adults.
But ferritin also rises with inflammation, like a vault guard who exaggerates. So in adults with infection or inflammation, WHO allows a higher cut-off: below 70.
Without iron, the marrow builds hemoglobin slowly. Red cells come out smaller and paler, and their sizes vary a lot — a wide RDW.
Fewer cells, small, pale and unequal: the classic iron-deficiency smear. Low ferritin is the test that clinches it.

scenes.title: The look-alike: thalassemia trait
scenes.altText: The smear morphs into thalassemia trait: cells stay small but become many and uniform, with a few target cells. A counter shows the RBC count high (about 5–7 million/µL). A Mentzer-index calculator appears: MCV ÷ RBC. Iron deficiency example: 72 ÷ 3.8 ≈ 18.9 (> 13). Thalassemia-trait example: 64 ÷ 5.9 ≈ 10.8 (< 13).

cues.text: Thalassemia trait also makes small cells — but for a different reason. The genes for one hemoglobin chain work at reduced output; iron is fine.
The marrow compensates by making MORE cells. So the RBC count is high, often 5 to 7 million, and the cells are small but even.
A quick screen is the Mentzer index: divide the MCV by the RBC count. Below 13 points to thalassemia trait; above 13 points to iron deficiency.
Iron deficiency example: MCV 72, RBC 3.8. 72 divided by 3.8 is about 18.9 — above 13.
Thalassemia trait example: MCV 64, RBC 5.9. 64 divided by 5.9 is about 10.8 — below 13. Next step: hemoglobin studies.

props.text: A screen only — confirm with lab tests

scenes.title: In the lab: the iron panel and HbA2
scenes.altText: A three-column comparison board fills in row by row for iron deficiency, anemia of inflammation and thalassemia trait: ferritin (low / normal-high / normal), TIBC-transferrin (high / low / normal), serum iron (low / low / normal), RBC count (low-normal / normal / high), MCV (low / normal or mildly low / low), and finally HbA2 > 3.5% marking β-thalassemia trait.

cues.text: The lab sorts small-cell anemias with an iron panel. Iron deficiency: ferritin low, serum iron low, and transferrin — the iron taxi — high, because the body makes more taxis to hunt for iron.
Anemia of inflammation: a hormone called hepcidin locks iron inside storage cells. Serum iron is low, but ferritin is normal or high, and transferrin is low.
It is usually a mild to moderate, normocytic anemia — small cells only if it lasts a long time.
Thalassemia trait: the iron panel is normal, the RBC count is high and the cells are small.
Hemoglobin studies confirm it. An HbA2 above 3.5 percent points to β-thalassemia trait.

scenes.title: Trap: low MCV is not always iron deficiency
scenes.altText: Trap card: “MCV is low, so it’s iron deficiency” is crossed out → “High RBC count + low MCV in a well patient → think thalassemia trait; check Mentzer index and HbA2.” A second card: “Ferritin is normal in a patient with arthritis, so iron deficiency is excluded” is crossed out → “Inflammation raises ferritin; WHO uses < 70 µg/L in adults with inflammation.”

cues.text: Trap: “The MCV is low, so it must be iron deficiency.” Not if the RBC count is high and the patient is well. Run the Mentzer index and check HbA2.
Trap two: “Ferritin is 45 in a patient with arthritis — normal, so iron deficiency is ruled out.” Inflammation pushes ferritin up, so WHO uses a higher cut-off, below 70, in adults with inflammation.
And the clincher pair: low ferritin means iron deficiency; HbA2 above 3.5 percent means β-thalassemia trait.

scenes.title: Many small soldiers vs few starving ones
scenes.altText: Memory aid: two armies. Left, a few thin, pale, mismatched soldiers with an empty pantry (“few starving soldiers — iron deficiency”). Right, a crowd of small, identical soldiers with a full pantry (“many small soldiers — thalassemia trait”). A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid: iron deficiency is a few starving soldiers — small, pale, mismatched, and the pantry, ferritin, is empty.
Thalassemia trait is many small soldiers — small but identical, more of them, and the pantry is full.
Where it breaks: the Mentzer index is only a screen and misclassifies some patients; both conditions can occur together; and inflammation can hide low iron behind a normal ferritin.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Ferritin < 15 µg/L (WHO) = iron deficiency”, “Mentzer < 13 + high RBC → thal trait”, “HbA2 > 3.5% confirms β-thal trait”.

cues.text: In a small-cell anemia, a low ferritin proves iron deficiency, while a high RBC count with a Mentzer index below 13 and an HbA2 above 3.5 percent points to β-thalassemia trait — so check before you prescribe iron.

props.label: Mentzer < 13 + high RBC → think thal trait

explanation.what: Plain language: small red cells can come from running out of iron or from an inherited, harmless gene change; the lab tells them apart with iron tests and a simple ratio. Scientific terms: microcytic anemia is most often iron deficiency (low ferritin) or thalassemia trait (normal iron studies, high RBC count, HbA2 > 3.5% in β-thalassemia trait); anemia of inflammation shows low serum iron with normal or high ferritin.
explanation.why: Without iron, hemoglobin synthesis slows, so cells are small, pale and variable in size, and stores (ferritin) empty first. In thalassemia trait, globin-chain output is reduced but iron is normal; the marrow makes more, smaller cells. In inflammation, hepcidin blocks iron absorption and traps iron in macrophages, and ferritin rises as an acute-phase protein.
explanation.measure: Ferritin (WHO: < 15 µg/L in apparently healthy adults; < 70 µg/L in adults with infection or inflammation), serum iron, transferrin/TIBC, RBC count, MCV, RDW and the Mentzer index (MCV ÷ RBC; < 13 suggests thalassemia trait, > 13 iron deficiency); HbA2 by HPLC or electrophoresis (> 3.5% in β-thalassemia trait).
explanation.differs: Iron deficiency (ferritin ↓, TIBC ↑, RBC ↓/normal, RDW ↑) vs thalassemia trait (iron normal, RBC ↑, Mentzer < 13, HbA2 ↑) vs anemia of inflammation (iron ↓, ferritin normal/↑, TIBC ↓, usually normocytic and mild-to-moderate).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the single best test for iron deficiency (ferritin), a Mentzer calculation, the trap of calling every low MCV iron deficiency, HbA2 > 3.5% for β-thal trait, and an inflamed patient whose “normal” ferritin hides iron deficiency.

comparisons.title: Iron deficiency vs thalassemia trait
comparisons.distinguisher: Ferritin and the RBC count (Mentzer index), then HbA2.

comparisons.title: Iron deficiency vs anemia of inflammation
comparisons.distinguisher: Ferritin and transferrin move in opposite directions.

mnemonic.text: Few starving soldiers vs many small soldiers.
mnemonic.explanation: Iron deficiency: few, small, pale, mismatched cells and empty iron stores. Thalassemia trait: many small, uniform cells with full stores.
mnemonic.limitation: The Mentzer index is only a screen and misclassifies some patients; iron deficiency and thalassemia trait can coexist; and inflammation can hide iron deficiency behind a normal ferritin. The aid does not cover HbA2 or anemia of inflammation.

analogyLimitations: The smear is schematic — real cells, target cells and pallor differ in appearance.
The worked MCV and RBC values are invented examples.
The “vault” and “taxi” images simplify iron storage and transport.
takeaway: In a small-cell anemia, a low ferritin proves iron deficiency, while a high RBC count with a Mentzer index below 13 and an HbA2 above 3.5 percent points to β-thalassemia trait — so check before you prescribe iron.

questions.stem: An otherwise healthy woman has Hb 9.6 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, RDW high and serum ferritin 8 µg/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Correct. A ferritin below the WHO cut-off of 15 µg/L in an apparently healthy adult diagnoses iron deficiency.
Incorrect. Thalassemia trait has normal ferritin and usually a high RBC count with uniform cells (normal RDW).
Incorrect. Inflammation gives normal or high ferritin.
Incorrect. B12 deficiency causes large (macrocytic) cells, not an MCV of 70.

questions.stem: A well man has MCV 66 fL and RBC 6.0 × 10¹²/L (6.0 million/µL). What does the Mentzer index suggest, and what is the next test?

options.text: Index 11 → thalassemia trait likely; measure HbA2 (and check iron studies)
options.rationale: Correct. 66 ÷ 6.0 = 11, below 13; HbA2 > 3.5% would support β-thalassemia trait.

options.text: Index 11 → iron deficiency likely; start iron
options.rationale: Incorrect. An index below 13 points toward thalassemia trait, not iron deficiency.
Incorrect. This multiplies instead of dividing (66 × 6.0).
Incorrect. This divides RBC by MCV; the index is MCV ÷ RBC.

questions.stem: A woman with active rheumatoid arthritis has a low serum iron, low transferrin saturation and a ferritin of 45 µg/L. How should the ferritin be interpreted?

options.text: Iron deficiency may still be present: inflammation raises ferritin, and WHO uses < 70 µg/L in adults with inflammation
options.rationale: Correct. Ferritin is an acute-phase protein; a value of 45 is below WHO’s inflammation cut-off.

options.text: Iron deficiency is excluded because 45 is above 15
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 15 µg/L cut-off applies to apparently healthy individuals, not to people with inflammation.
Incorrect. Iron overload is suggested by much higher ferritin values, not 45 µg/L.

options.text: Ferritin cannot be used at all in inflammation
options.rationale: Incorrect. It can be used with a higher cut-off or with inflammation-marker adjustment.

references.citation: World Health Organization. WHO guideline on use of ferritin concentrations to assess iron status in individuals and populations. Geneva: WHO; 2020.
references.usedFor: Ferritin is a good marker of iron stores; cut-off < 15 µg/L for iron deficiency in apparently healthy adults; in adults with infection or inflammation < 70 µg/L may indicate iron deficiency (conditional recommendation).

references.citation: Tabassum S, Khakwani M, Fayyaz A, Taj N. Role of Mentzer index for differentiating iron deficiency anemia and beta thalassemia trait in pregnant women. Pak J Med Sci. 2022;38(4 Part-II):878-882.
references.usedFor: Mentzer index = MCV ÷ RBC; > 13 suggests IDA, < 13 βTT; sensitivity/specificity 91%/83% (IDA) and 83%/91% (βTT) in one population; HbA2 > 3.5% used to confirm β-thalassemia trait.

references.citation: Weiss G, Ganz T, Goodnough LT. Anemia of inflammation. Blood. 2019;133(1):40-50.
references.usedFor: AI is mild-to-moderate, normochromic and normocytic; hepcidin degrades ferroportin, trapping iron in macrophages and blocking absorption; low serum iron, reduced transferrin, normal or increased ferritin; ferritin < 30 µg/L associated with true iron deficiency.

claims.text: WHO: ferritin < 15 µg/L indicates iron deficiency in apparently healthy adults; < 70 µg/L may be used in adults with infection or inflammation.
Mentzer index = MCV ÷ RBC; < 13 suggests thalassemia trait, > 13 iron deficiency; it is a screen, not a diagnosis.
Anemia of inflammation: mild-to-moderate, usually normocytic; hepcidin traps iron; low serum iron and transferrin with normal or high ferritin.

claims.note: Arithmetic with the cited formula; values invented.

claims.text: Reviewer figures: ferritin < 12 µg/L diagnostic; < 50–60 in inflammation predicts iron response; transferrin saturation < 15%; transferrin/TIBC high and RDW high in IDA; thal-trait RBC 5–7 M/µL; iron deficiency lowers HbA2; AI hemoglobin rarely < 8 g/dL.
